question: What is the diamond problem in multiple inheritance?
caps: c dot Scanner double colon id

scenes.sub: Two paths to the same base class, and two copies of it.
scenes.say: The diamond problem. It happens when a class inherits the same base class through two different paths. Let's build one.

scenes.head: The shape that gives it its name
scenes.say: A Device has an id. Scanner and Printer both inherit from Device. A Copier is both a scanner and a printer, so it inherits from both. Draw the hierarchy, and you get a diamond.

scenes.head: Inside a Copier: two Devices

steps.cue: c dot Scanner double colon id

scenes.say: With ordinary inheritance, each path brings its own base. So one Copier object contains two separate Device sub objects, each with its own id. Now c dot id is ambiguous. The compiler can't know which id you mean, so it's a compile error. You can name the path, c dot Scanner double colon id, but you still have two ids that can drift apart. Converting a Copier pointer to a Device pointer is ambiguous too.

scenes.head: The fix: virtual inheritance
scenes.say: The fix is virtual inheritance. Scanner and Printer inherit virtually from Device, so the final object holds exactly one Device, and both parts point to that shared copy. Now c dot id just works. The cost is a little extra indirection, because the shared base's position is found at run time.

scenes.head: Follow-up: who constructs the shared base?
scenes.say: A classic follow up: who constructs the shared base? Scanner and Printer each try to pass an id to Device. But with a virtual base, the most derived class constructs it directly, here Copier, and the middle classes' calls are ignored. So c dot id is three. If Copier didn't call a Device constructor, it would need a default one.

lines: Diamond: a class inherits one base through two paths.
Normal inheritance gives two base copies: ambiguous names and conversions.
virtual inheritance shares one copy; the most-derived class constructs it.
scenes.say: The diamond problem: a class inherits the same base through two paths. With normal inheritance you get two copies of the base, and names become ambiguous. Virtual inheritance shares a single copy, which the most derived class constructs.
